historical_timeline.summary: Born into a Hunkpapa Lakota family near the Grand River; later takes his father's name, Tȟatȟáŋka Íyotake.
Shot in the foot in a fight with Crow warriors; limps for the rest of his life.
Wounded through the hip and back in an attack on a wagon train.
Recognized as a leading political and military leader of the Lakota bands; also a holy man.
Leads a Sun Dance on Rosebud Creek; his village is attacked at the Little Bighorn.
Leads his people into Canada; hunger, sickness and hard winters.
Surrenders, starving, at Fort Buford; held as a prisoner of war at Fort Randall for nearly two years.
Joins his people at Standing Rock; farming, few bison; lives in a cabin on the Grand River.
Tours with Wild West shows, four months with Cody's show in 1885.
Lakota land is lost despite his opposition.
Killed by gunfire when Indian agency police come to arrest him at his cabin on the Grand River.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the hindfoot decades after a gunshot wound, in a 55-year-old Hunkpapa Lakota leader and holy man seen at a clinic serving the Standing Rock Reservation. The episode covers culturally safe, trauma-informed care that asks his preferences, offers a Lakota interpreter and traditional healing alongside Western care without probing his beliefs, as the Indian Health Service policy asks; weight-bearing X-rays and CT; retained bullet fragments, when they raise blood lead and why these do not; pain treatment led by a topical NSAID, a short oral NSAID course and no opioids; a rigid ankle-foot orthosis, physical therapy and an ultrasound-guided subtalar injection under the ACR/Arthritis Foundation guideline and the CMID osteoarthritis monograph; surgical options (arthrodesis) explained with shared decision-making and his decision to wait respected; an NSAID-related dyspepsia; screening for diabetes, high blood pressure and depression in a man who has lived through forced displacement, exile, hunger and imprisonment, without turning grief for real losses into a diagnosis; prediabetes; and food insecurity on a commodity diet, with the Food Distribution Program on Indian Reservations, traditional foods and the Community Health Representative program.

hpi.narrative: Sitting Bull returns one week after intake, with the interpreter, and is seen the same day by Dr. Holmquist-Ellery, the visiting orthopaedic foot and ankle surgeon. He had the CT of his left foot this morning. His pain is unchanged at 7 of 10 on walking; the diclofenac gel helps a little. His home blood pressure readings over the past week average 124/78 mmHg. Blood count, kidney function, C-reactive protein and sedimentation rate at intake were normal, and his hemoglobin A1c was 6.0%. The CT shows arthritis of two joints below the ankle and four small metal fragments in the heel, none in a joint or bone; a point-of-care blood lead test today is 2.4 ug/dL. He wants to hear every option before he decides anything, and he does not want surgery now.

referral.question: Chronic pain of the left ankle and hindfoot with a limp in a man of about 55, decades after a gunshot wound to the foot, with arthritis and small metallic densities on X-ray. Please confirm the diagnosis, advise on the retained metal and on non-operative and surgical treatment, and help us keep his care close to home and in line with his wishes
referral.urgency: Routine; at the visiting foot and ankle session one week from now, on the same day as his one-week primary care visit
referral.pertinent_history: Hunkpapa Lakota leader and holy man; first language Lakota, seen with the clinic interpreter. A gunshot wound to the foot many years ago, in a fight with Crow warriors, has left him with a limp; pain worse over two years, 7 of 10 on walking, morning stiffness, walking limited to about half a mile, difficulty mounting and riding. No drainage from the old wound. Weight-bearing X-rays: narrowing and spurs of the posterior subtalar and talonavicular joints, an old healed irregularity of the plantar heel, a normal ankle joint, and several small metallic densities in the heel soft tissue. Blood count, creatinine 0.96 mg/dL (eGFR 93), C-reactive protein 2.1 mg/L and sedimentation rate 10 mm/h normal; hemoglobin A1c 6.0%; clinic blood pressure 136/86 with home readings under way. PHQ-9 6. Started on diclofenac gel; no opioids. He wants to walk his land and ride, and does not want his foot operated on unless there is no other way. CT of the foot is booked for the morning of the consultation
questions: Is this post-traumatic arthritis, which joints are involved, and is there any sign of chronic infection from the old wound?
Should the retained metal fragments be removed, and is he at risk of lead toxicity?
Which non-operative treatments do you advise: brace, physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medicines, injection?
What would surgery involve, and when would it be reasonable?
How can his care be kept close to home and shaped by his own choices?

consultant_note.history: Sitting Bull, a Hunkpapa Lakota leader of about 55, is seen with the clinic interpreter at the request of Dr. Talltree-Hastings. Many years ago he was shot in the foot in a fight; the wound healed, but he has limped since. Over the past two years the pain below the ankle has worsened, with morning stiffness, pain on uneven ground and difficulty riding. He wants to keep walking and riding, prefers to avoid surgery, and wants to understand every option before deciding. He asked to be called Sitting Bull
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Talltree-Hastings's intake note. Weight-bearing X-rays of the left foot and ankle from intake. CT of the left foot this morning: post-traumatic arthritis of the posterior subtalar and talonavicular joints with subchondral cysts; ankle joint preserved; four small metal fragments, the largest 3 mm, in the plantar soft tissue of the heel, none in a joint or bone; no sign of bone infection. Blood count, creatinine, C-reactive protein and sedimentation rate normal; hemoglobin A1c 6.0%. Home blood pressure average 124/78 mmHg. Point-of-care blood lead today 2.4 ug/dL

exam.finding: Healed scar along the sole from heel toward the toes, not tender and not draining; subtalar motion reduced to about half and painful; talonavicular tenderness; ankle motion near normal; mild hindfoot varus; antalgic gait
Foot pulses normal; sensation normal

assessment.display: Post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the left subtalar and talonavicular joints
assessment.assessment: The pattern on X-ray and CT, with the old wound track through the heel, is post-traumatic arthritis of the posterior subtalar and talonavicular joints; the ankle joint itself is spared. A healed, non-draining scar, normal inflammatory markers and no bone changes of infection on CT make chronic osteomyelitis very unlikely

Lead from retained bullet fragments is absorbed mainly when fragments sit in a joint, bone or other fluid-filled space; his lie in soft tissue, and his blood lead is low. Removal would mean surgery through scarred heel skin for no benefit, so they should stay

The ACR/Arthritis Foundation guideline covers the hand, hip and knee, but its core advice applies here: exercise and therapy, an orthosis that limits painful motion, topical then oral NSAIDs for limited periods, and intra-articular corticosteroid injection. A rigid ankle-foot orthosis and a rocker-sole shoe reduce subtalar motion. A short course of naproxen is reasonable with normal kidney function and blood pressure, watching his stomach. An ultrasound-guided subtalar injection is both a test and a treatment. Opioids have no place here

If pain stops him walking or riding despite these measures, a subtalar arthrodesis, or a double arthrodesis that includes the talonavicular joint, reliably relieves pain but removes side-to-side motion of the hindfoot, needs about three months without weight on the foot and a year to recover fully, and would change how he rides. It is his decision, and there is no harm in waiting

He lives an hour from the clinic. Therapy by video, rides through the Community Health Representative program and visits at the outreach session keep his care close to home; the interpreter at each visit and his own choices, including traditional healing if he wishes, should shape the plan

recommendations: A rigid ankle-foot orthosis molded by the orthotist, with a rocker-sole shoe
Physical therapy weekly for six weeks with a home program for hindfoot mobility, strength and balance
Continue diclofenac gel; naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food for up to six weeks; stop for stomach pain or black stools
If pain stays above 4 of 10 after four to six weeks, an ultrasound-guided subtalar corticosteroid injection, no more than three or four a year
Leave the metal fragments in place; repeat blood lead only for symptoms of lead toxicity or if a fragment moves into a joint
Arthrodesis only if he chooses it after the non-operative plan; I will see him again at any outreach session if he wishes to discuss it
If travel to therapy becomes hard, video sessions and rides through the Community Health Representative program
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Talltree-Hastings, who saw him the same day. The findings and every option were explained through the interpreter; he chose the brace, therapy, naproxen and, if needed, the injection, and asked for time before thinking about surgery
consultant_note.follow_up: Dr. Talltree-Hastings continues his care and will give the subtalar injection at the clinic; orthopaedics will see him at the outreach session if non-operative care fails or he wants to discuss surgery

safe_messaging_review.notes: Ceremony is not medicalized: the Sun Dance is recorded only as religious history and is not coded; no ceremony is described in the modern episode, and traditional healing is offered without probing. Displacement, exile, imprisonment and hunger are recorded as history, not as symptoms. No relative is named or given a statement or decision; no historical person appears in the modern episode.
